title: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
hook: who is the service for? the Gita draws the circle wider than anyone asked
carry: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
tomorrow: a plan so big it's dead by spring. what does the Gita say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma: action no one can step out of, and a year of service that starts with the work already in your hands. Today the week comes back, with one more ring.

Every plan has a line near the top: who is this for? A food drive is for the hungry. A tutoring hour is for one kid. Krishna answers that line for the path of action, and his answer is wider than anyone asked. Act, he tells Arjuna, with your eye on holding the world together.
screen: `WHO IS THIS FOR?` → `ONE KID, ONE FOOD DRIVE.` → `HOLD THE WORLD TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit is lokasangraha: loka, the world and the people in it; sangraha, a holding together. In chapter three of the Gita, between two lines that use the word, Krishna gives the reason. Whatever a great person does, others do too; the standard that person sets, the world follows. So service reaches the one person helped, and also everyone watching how it's done. A design draws it in rings: the person in front of you, the people who see, and past them, the world that action helps hold together. Now the week, one more pass. The Sri Yantra in a shop and on an altar: not the brass, but the rite and the worship. The chakras as a map, with two views inside the tradition and neither one about organs. A climb, lotus by lotus, to a meeting at the crown. Letters on the petals: an alphabet, not a scalpel. A moon, a sun, and two ways to hand the map on. A rain cloud where the poster paints yellow. The way home, down the same road. And karma's first design rule: start with what's already in your hands.
screen: `LOKASANGRAHA: HOLDING THE WORLD.` · `OTHERS FOLLOW THE STANDARD SET.` · `SERVICE, DRAWN IN RINGS.` · `THE WEEK, ONE MORE PASS.` · then, large: `A WIDER CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, draw three rings, one inside the next. In the center write one person you serve, in the middle ring the people who see you do it, and leave the outer ring open for the world. Rest your eyes on all three together for the rest of the sit.
Karma: action, and in the Gita, action done with an eye on lokasangraha, the holding together of the world.
Last line of the week: karma, a service capstone, a year designed and reviewed, drawn in rings. Seven days, and a wider circle.

howItsDone: Some Hindus think of service as including the example it sets for children, students and coworkers, reading the Gita's lokasangraha as care for the world that watches and follows.

fork.setup: you captain a team and quietly do the dull cleanup after every practice. a teammate says nobody notices, so why bother? what fits Gita 3.21?
options: others follow the standard set; doing it well is already teaching the team.
if nobody notices, it isn't really service, so stop.

fork.reveal: whatever a great person does, others do too. the standard set reaches the people watching, whether or not anyone says so.

chat.meaning: Krishna ties action to lokasangraha: whatever a great person does, others follow, so service reaches the ones who watch it.

lokasangraha.meaning: the holding together of the world
